item.title: Ransomware Recovery Firm Founder Charged With Wire Fraud
item.description:
Ransomware Recovery Firm Founder Charged With Wire Fraud

Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, co-founder of the Florida-based ransomware recovery firm RansomwareHelp, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation revealed that the company routinely paid ransomware attackers for decryption keys while claiming to victims that it used proprietary cryptographic tools.

🔍 The Allegations

The indictment, returned in Rhode Island, alleges that the 52-year-old Miami-based co-founder routinely paid ransomware groups for decryption keys and charged victims a significant markup for work that was never actually performed. RansomwareHelp, a six-year-old Florida business, had claimed on its website that it used “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems. The company explicitly stated it did not promote, intermediate, or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of its clients.

⚙️ FBI Sting Operation

The FBI set up a sting operation in which investigators posed as both a ransomware victim company and a fictitious ransomware group. Investigators, acting as victims, supplied the company with a phony ransomware note and expressed a desire not to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp initially reiterated its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments.

However, Palacio soon contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for a decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of 0.2 bitcoin, or around $13,000. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly informed the fake victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and quoted a decryption cost of $13,260. The following day, the indictment states, Palacio messaged the fictitious group to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The agreed-upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, yet Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including a $2,750 diagnostic fee and the $13,260 full fee.

💡 Real-World Impact

In 2024, Paul Ihme, co-founder of the security firm Soteria, heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection. RansomwareHelp sent a proposal for a recovery price of $438,880, claiming this included “professional configuration of forensic servers” and “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms.”

The proposal claimed the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.” Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network using Anydesk remote desktop software in part to delete copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers. A review of the network found only one copy of the ransom note, unearthed from a backup snapshot. When the security firm connected to the Lockbit chat server using the provided user ID, they discovered RansomwareHelp had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days, pleading not to reveal their involvement to the victim.

#Ransomware #FBI #WireFraud #Cybersecurity #LawEnforcement

Source: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

item.title: JPMorgan Chase Warns of Data Breach via Third-Party Cyberattack
item.description:
JPMorgan Chase Warns of Data Breach via Third-Party Cyberattack

J.P. Morgan Chase announced that it suffered a data breach following a cyberattack on a third-party service provider, which exposed customers’ personal information and marketing data. The bank stated that its services were not disrupted and the incident is unrelated to a service disruption that occurred earlier in the week.

🏦 Banking Sector Impact

J.P. Morgan Chase Bank is the largest U.S. bank by assets, with about $4.1 trillion as of June 2026, and its consumer banking division reports about 78 million active digital customers. The bank’s announcement on X stated, “We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack.” The bank further disclosed, “Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.”

💳 Payment Networks Affected

Visa and Mastercard confirmed that they were involved in third-party incidents, though both have not confirmed any impact on customers or their core payment networks.

  • Visa: A spokesperson told BleepingComputer that the incident is “associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific.” Visa stated, “Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected.”
  • Mastercard: The company confirmed it was “informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program.” A spokesperson assured that “There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards.”

🏭 Third-Party Provider

On November 11, 2026, the n0n ransomware group claimed responsibility for an attack on Qubole, a cloud data analytics company owned by Idera, suspected to be the third-party provider used by the financial institutions. Qubole is used for cloud data analytics, automated processing, real-time analysis, and reporting.

📊 Stolen Data and Extortion

Between October 14 and 26, 2026, the n0n ransomware group allegedly used compromised Qubole credentials to access customers’ AWS environments through IAM roles configured to grant Qubole access. The group claimed to have stolen 53.9 GB across 30,743 files directly from Qubole, including customer contracts, pricing records, staff and trial-user information, and production data. Additionally, they claimed to hold nearly one petabyte of data from Qubole’s customer networks. The n0n group leaked the claimed data on its extortion site on November 16, 2026, stating that their extortion demands were ignored after contacting Qubole and the affected companies.

#JPMorganChase #Ransomware #Cybersecurity #Qubole #DataBreach #VisaMastercard

Source: Vendor data breach exposes Chase, Visa, Mastercard customer info

item.title: NVIDIA Investigates Third-Party Partner Incident Following Gentlemen Ransomware Claims
item.description:
NVIDIA Investigates Third-Party Partner Incident Following Gentlemen Ransomware Claims

NVIDIA is investigating claims of a security breach after the Gentlemen ransomware group added the company to its dark web data leak site, though no proof of the breach has been shared yet.

🔍 Overview

  • The Gentlemen ransomware group listed NVIDIA on its dark web data leak site and threatened to release data with a countdown ending in nine days on November 28.
  • NVIDIA stated it has not found evidence that its systems were compromised, but is looking into a separate incident that may have affected a third-party partner.
  • An NVIDIA spokesperson told BleepingComputer: “We have found no indication that NVIDIA systems or networks were affected. We continue to monitor the situation.”

⚙️ Key details

  • The Gentlemen surfaced last year as a closed ransomware group before switching to a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) model.
  • The group offers affiliates up to a 90% cut of ransom proceeds.
  • It operates as a double-extortion group that exfiltrates sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to leak the information.
  • Since emerging, The Gentlemen has claimed more than 1,100 victims across manufacturing, healthcare, transportation, energy, education, and financial services sectors.

#NVIDIA #Ransomware #Cybersecurity #DataBreach

Source: NVIDIA investigating Gentlemen ransomware breach claims

item.title: Ransomware Defense: Detecting Pre-Encryption Attack Stages
item.description:
Ransomware Defense: Detecting Pre-Encryption Attack Stages

Ransomware attacks rarely begin with the ransomware payload itself. Operators first need an initial foothold, and common entry paths include exploitation of vulnerable internet-facing systems, abuse of stolen credentials, and social engineering. By the time encryption occurs, the intrusion may already include credential theft, privilege escalation, defense evasion, recovery sabotage, lateral movement, and data exfiltration. In data-extortion attacks, encryption may never happen at all, as operators steal data and threaten to leak it without encrypting anything.

🚀 Initial Entry Paths

Attacker entry into environments typically occurs through three primary vectors:

  • Vulnerable Systems: Unpatched, externally accessible services provide a route into the environment.
  • Stolen Credentials: Compromised credentials allow attackers to enter through legitimate remote-access or cloud services.
  • Social Engineering: This path targets users and the processes surrounding identity and access.

Once attackers establish access, they use stolen credentials and legitimate administration tools to move through victim environments before deploying ransomware.

🔍 Pre-Encryption Detection Signals

Defenders need to detect behaviors that precede encryption, not only the encryptor itself. Five high-value signals deserve immediate attention when monitoring for suspicious post-compromise behavior:

Signal Description
Defense tampering Attempts to stop security services, modify protection agents, load vulnerable drivers, or clear event logs.
Privilege escalation and lateral movement Unexpected privileged accounts, remote-execution tools spreading across hosts, or unusual server-to-server remote access.
Data exfiltration Unusual outbound transfers from systems that do not normally upload large volumes of data.
Recovery sabotage Deletion of shadow copies, backup catalogs, or recovery options using tools such as vssadmin.exe, wbadmin.exe, or bcdedit.exe.
Pre-encryption file behavior Rapid file enumeration, repeated read-write-rename activity, and encryption-like changes across local or network locations.

⚙️ Layered Defense Strategy

Stopping ransomware is rarely about a single control. A comprehensive strategy requires reducing opportunities for initial compromise, detecting and containing malicious activity when they do occur, and having a reliable way to recover if systems or data are affected.

  • Prevention: Reducing unnecessary internet exposure, prioritizing patching of high-risk systems, strengthening identity and access controls, and protecting email and collaboration channels.
  • Detection and Response: Monitoring endpoints for suspicious post-compromise behavior provides a layer when preventive controls do not stop the initial intrusion. Endpoint protection, email security, and extended detection and response (XDR) tools can identify and contain malicious activity across endpoints, email, and the wider environment.
  • Recovery: Integrated backup and recovery provide the path to restoring affected systems and data. It is important to note that this layer does not undo data theft, a critical distinction in double-extortion attacks.

#Ransomware #Cybersecurity #ThreatDetection #DataExfiltration

Source: Five warning signs of ransomware breach before encryption or data theft
